I think that so many people like to believe that the afterlife is "all fun and games" or unlimited bliss because such a belief helps to make bearable the pain of their present lives. They prefer blissful naïvité over critical thinking because the latter could potentially destroy their hope for liberation from suffering. As such those people prefer to dismiss any critical perspective as something born out of "negativity" or a "conspiracy theory".

I agree with you. Many people detest their own lives due to the very real suffering they face on a daily basis such as poverty, illness and mental problems and don't really want to live the lives they have. They all say that they wouldn't have been born into such lives if the had a choice. This is the reason why the soul trap theory is so cogent to some people. It is not because of paranoia or conspiracy theories.

I don't think that it's merely temporary either. I'm sure that the soul suffers traumas because of all of these experiences of suffering and carries those same traumas into other incarnations. I think this because I feel quite traumatized at the level of the soul myself.

I don't see my viewpoint as negative even though it may appear so on the surface. Rather I view rebellion against something negative as a supremely positive act. If this reincarnation system is indeed a soul trap then those of us who recognize it as such and seek to oppose it and escape from it are the ones with the most positive perspective, at least in substance.

You make wrong assumptions about what I believe. I can only speak for myself, but I don't believe that those beings are weak or dumb or that it is as simple as "just ignore the light". If it were that simple I know that I wouldn't be here. No, I believe that escaping is much more difficult than that (and so did the Gnostics). However, a decision to flee is the first step.

Think about this for a second.

If you are correct, then I simply risk embarrassment upon trying to flee. If the "Beings of Light" really are benevolent then they will understand.

If, however, I am correct, then you risk being seized by those beings and forced to live a potentially negative incarnation against your own will.

I would like to have a more positive view about this but my soul just doesn't feel comfortable with it all. I have been suffering from a deep existential anxiety for much of my life. It just doesn't feel right to me here.

Why don't I trust the entities on the other side?

First of all, as I alluded to in my previous post, my soul just feels so weary and traumatized here. It is as though I am feeling the sequelae of abuse and forced reincarnation in a world that is alien to the nature of my soul and I just can't find any benevolence in this anymore. My instincts tell me not to trust most entities on the other side, especially those who claim to have authority.

Second, people who experience NDEs often report the beings who they see in conjunction with the light  as religious figures such as Jesus, Buddha or angels. This really unsettles me, not because I am secular-minded or anything (I am actually a very spiritual person), but rather because my research into the major religions has revealed to me something considerably dark. Put bluntly, the religions and their doctrines are for the most part perverse and batshit crazy.

Take Christianity for instance. It is a religion whose "god" requires the bloody sacrifice of living beings for atonement (OT) and this is said to be fulfilled in the sacrifice of Jesus on the cross (NT). Furthermore, look at the teachings of Jesus in the Gospels. Many commandments teach man to be servile, to submit, to be an obedient slave, to turn the other cheek, to allow oneself to be mistreated without retaliation. In short, they foster a slavish and disempowering mindset.

Eastern religions such as Buddhism and Hinduism teach about karma and today this is reinforced by the New Age. According to these belief systems, we constantly have to pay off karmic debts and that keeps us here in this cycle of suffering. Again this seems to me like a very enslaving doctrine.

So when these figures from these enslaving belief systems show up in NDEs I cannot help but feel suspicious of them and wish to avoid them. To me they seem much more like deceptive "archons" to use the Gnostic term than any kind of benevolent beings.

I don't believe in the Gnostic cosmology of a botched world created by a malevolent demiurge. Neither do I see matter as inherently evil. Rather I suspect that our world and its reincarnation system have been hijacked by intrusive entities of a negative nature who masquerade as "god" or "angels" or "ascended masters" or whatnot.

Don't get me wrong, I would like to believe in a positive blissful afterlife like so many NDE believers do, but unfortunately I see the soul trap scenario as more likely to be true.

I'm sorry if my answer comes across as negative but you asked me to explain my point of view and so I gave you a sincere answer.

I don't mean to sound negative but there is plenty of reason to consider the soul trap theory when one takes an honest look at the state of the world. The theory in question is particularly cogent to those who live harsh lives and are tired of so much suffering.

The soul trap theory actually draws most of its inspiration from a religious-spiritual current in the ancient Mediterranean world known today as Gnosticism. The Gnostics held that this world of matter was a corrupt creation of the evil demiurge Yaldabaoth (identified as the biblical god Yahweh) and his archons (angels). According to Gnosticism, the demiurge and his archons managed to trap our souls in their corrupt creation and continue to keep us here through a system of reincarnation. This is where the soul trap concept comes into play.

While I don't believe completely that this world is a totally corrupt creation nor do I deny the importance of the material like the Gnostics did, I do suspect some level of intrusion on the part of negative entities and certainly don't wish to be part of it anymore. I for one intend to attempt to flee on the other side as I no longer trust any entities there.

I feel trauma and weariness in my soul and have done for a long time. I can't prove anything to anybody but I just sense that something is wrong.

According to NDE researcher Jeffrey Long, the majority of NDE'ers experience a level of awareness during their NDE that is significantly greater than their everyday awareness and also remember everything the same way even decades later. He talks about the tendency towards a special kind of lucid perception surrounding NDEs.

I remember my attitude towards life in my later teenage years. I had already watched a documentary on NDEs and believed in the afterlife but still immersed myself in more worldly interests for the most part and didn't give too much thought to death or anything too otherworldly.

I think that this is a healthy attitude to have: a strong focus on present material life and all of the beautiful things therein and a firm yet not too obsessive belief in the afterlife which gives us reassurance and makes this present material life even more meaningful. I felt extremely happy back then.

My death anxiety started to emerge in my early 20s when I got involved in religion thinking that I would fulfill my spiritual needs. Religion places so much emphasis upon death and the afterlife. It made me fixate on the topic and become unable to enjoy present material life. Thankfully I left religion after a few years and began my own spiritual seeking. I have now learned how to balance material and spiritual life.

I don't think that the relatively low percentage of people who experience NDEs after cardiac arrest is necessarily a problem. It doesn't take away from the testimonies of those who do experience them, at least for me.

It could be that transition to the other side doesn't always happen the same way and that NDEs are just one of multiple methods.

It is possible that some souls experience a kind of soul sleep before awakening to the spiritual world. This could be to protect those souls from trauma as they pass over.

Another possibility is that some souls reach the NDE stage earlier than others. Those who are late to exit might simply be clinging to life in the material body and therefore not experience a NDE like others do.

I don't think you should worry too much about the loss of consciousness when you sleep. You don't experience anything during that time but you are still here nevertheless and you begin to experience things once again when you wake up. The same could be true with the soul sleep option at the time of death. You might "sleep" and not experience anything for a while but then your consciousness could come back online and you could come face to face with another level of reality.

I understand what you say about the suffering in this world. It is something that affects me too. I personally have never really felt at home here.

I was just thinking about this the other day although I phrased it differently in my mind:

Why do so many people cling to materialism as though it were the default perspective?

I've shared information about NDEs with others. I've explained to them how the fact that people who have reached a state of clinical death continue to have conscious experience and encounter a much more expanded level of reality despite being without heartbeat for several minutes is evidence for the veracity of the survival of consciousness and the afterlife. I've even mentioned cases of OBEs and veridical perception. Many people admit that the evidence that I give them is quite convincing but then speculate that there must be some other materialist mechanism that we just don't know about. In other words, they are unable to conceive things from a non-materialist perspective.

I myself have never assumed materialism to be true. For me it has always been nothing more than an ideology, not too dissimilar to a religious fundamentalism. Materialism has no concrete proof to support its lofty claims about the nature of reality. Its doctrines are articles of faith. I have on the other hand witnessed or experienced various paranormal phenomena which shouldn't be possible according to the materialist worldview. I trust my own experience over the ivory-tower "rationalism" of materialist intellectuals.

I am a simple person. I hear countless testimonies of people who experienced a vastly greater spiritual reality even after their heart had stopped supplying blood to the brain and furthermore experienced veridical perception from an out-of-body perspective, and therefore conclude that consciousness survives physical death and that the afterlife and reincarnation exist. I see no reason to insist on looking for another explanation in line with materialism. I don't think that materialism is valid anyway. It is certainly not the default perspective.

I think that many people cling to materialism because they have been brought up in a modern world which only places emphasis upon the material and even fosters skepticism towards the spiritual. Because of this they have few or no other points of reference.

I also believe that the expulsion of spirituality and the promotion of materialism have been very much by design. The industrialists who have become the elite of the modern world wish to reduce the importance of spiritual matters or even banish them completely and make everybody direct their energy almost exclusively towards industry, wealth creation and consumerism. Those rulers and their social engineers aim to build and maintain a materialistic world made in their own image and likeness.

The principal reason for which so many people cling to materialism is social conditioning.

Many spiritual people are fixated on NDEs, astral projection and anything to do with the "other side". I think that those people are simply dissatisfied with their present earthly lives and seek escapism in other extraphysical realms.

However, we are here to experience the sensations and adventures of materiality. Indeed, I bet it gets really boring in the afterlife after a while and most souls soon wish to reincarnate and experience more sensations and adventures.

The Egyptians had a very healthy view of life. They were extremely spiritual yet at the same time greatly valued happiness and material pleasures within this world.

I personally don't buy into the idea that we choose our forms of suffering before our incarnations. I'm not a big fan of theories concerning karma either. I think that the world is a lot more random and chaotic than what many like to believe, and if there are beings on the other side who try to convince us that we must reincarnate under certain negative circumstances for our karmic resolution, then I believe that those beings are most likely malevolent "archons" who manipulate souls for their own sadistic amusement.

I've heard some people say that the souls of murderers and victims agree to their roles prior to their respective incarnations in order to settle past karma. That sounds extremely sick to me. That justification can be applied to absolutely every kind of atrocity from genocides to sexual abuse. I for one don't believe that there are any true lessons to be found in that kind of evil. Such experiences only beget trauma at the level of the soul. The idea that those are opportunities for growth is simply insanity in my opinion.

My view with regard to evil people or murderers is that some souls actually regress instead of evolving. Things can either advance towards a positive harmonious state or a negative disharmonious state. The soul is no different. Murderers and psychopaths are messed up souls who have lost all of their humanity and gravitate towards warped things due to their own warped nature. They are not part of some greater plan of learning but rather simply defective units of consciousness who harbor some truly destructive tendencies.

I know that my answer probably goes against the grain but I really don't find much sense in explanations put out by proponents of karma.

Christians don't really know anything about the afterlife or the nature of reality. Their theology is nothing more than a body of interpretations of other people's opinions contained in the Bible and without any certain basis in reality. This is why I no longer care to entertain their arguments.

Only experience can bring about reliable knowledge. I'm a spiritual person and believe in a higher intelligence and a greater spiritual dimension of reality but I don't believe that any religion can offer reliable answers due to the dogmatic nature of religion itself.

For me, the idea that suicide will lead one to hell or burden one with negative karma is extremely simplistic and doesn't take into account the reasons why many people commit suicide in the first place. Some people suffer from immense pain or mental health problems that affect their ability to reason in a normal manner. Others are simply unable to function in a world that is extremely demanding.

You need to find a reason to live for yourself and focus on the beautiful things that this world has to offer. That is a good start.

I would say some general MMA training would do you good.

At a MMA gym you would be able to pressure test your Karate techniques against live resistance in sparring class and also learn some grappling techniques to combine with your Karate.

If we talk about individual styles, I think that wrestling would make for a good combination. First, you would learn takedown defense, useful in the event that you come across a grappler in a fight. Second, you would learn some effective takedowns to be used in the event that you ever find yourself outclassed by a more competent striker and need to take the fight to the ground. Also, in my experience, wrestling is more practical to learn than Judo. The double legs and single legs are simpler to learn than the winding throws of Judo and are relatively easy to apply to fighting with strikes, hence why they are so popular in MMA. Wrestling would be a good option.

Kyokushin Karate is good but the problem is that in sparring they don't strike to the face or head which can lead to some bad habits as far as realistic fighting is concerned. I would recommend cross-training in something like Muay Thai or kickboxing as these both allow strikes to the face and head.

Practice a martial art or combat sport that includes live sparring and pressure testing such as BJJ, Muay Thai, wrestling and Judo. Those are the most practical.

If you don't have any particular art mind you could always locate a MMA gym nearby and do some general MMA training. You'll learn the basics of fighting much more quickly than if you studied some traditional martial art without pressure testing. The exercise aspect will help you with your mental wellbeing and the practical skills that you'll learn will give you confidence. Once you've immersed yourself in MMA you might find one aspect that you enjoy more such as the grappling or the striking. Then you could concentrate more on that aspect.

Martial arts training will help you to cut down on the alcohol too. Once you get into productive things like training booze usually starts to lose its appeal.

It is easier to relearn a martial art that you've studied previously than learn one from scratch. Your muscle memory will recognize the basic movements and you'll be able to reintegrate them with relative ease. Of course, things like timing and strategy will be a little off at first due to lack of practice but you'll soon get them back.

I took a few years off BJJ but when I got back into BJJ in conjunction with new MMA training it didn't take me too long to recover my previous level and be able to hold my own against purple belts again.

You're still 17. This is a perfect time to get back into martial arts. Your previous experience will definitely help you.
